paragraphs: Here's what I think this whole passage is about, friend: remembering before you give. The worshiper doesn't just drop off a basket. He stands before the priest and tells the story: a wandering father, hard labor in Egypt, a God who "heard our voice and saw our affliction, toil, and oppression" (Deuteronomy 26:7). By the time that basket hits the altar, it's not a payment, it's a thank-you note with fruit in it.

And look who gets to eat: the worshiper rejoices with the Levite and the foreigner living among them (Deuteronomy 26:11), and the third-year tithe goes to the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow, "that they may eat and be filled within your gates" (Deuteronomy 26:12). The good things God gave were meant to reach them too. Then the giver says, "I have done everything You commanded me" (Deuteronomy 26:14). Friend, that is a LOT of faithful little steps, and each one was an act of worship.

Then Moses brings it home: follow these commands with all your heart and all your soul (Deuteronomy 26:16). The LORD calls Israel His "treasured possession" (Deuteronomy 26:18), and that is the people being asked to obey. So here's your question, baker: when you give, serve or obey, are you remembering who rescued you first? This sermon isn't finished yet, and neither is Moses.
